newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian cabinet sworn in after confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Romanian cabinet sworn in after confidence vote.

text.p: A reformist government forged from a political deal to overturn Romania's post-Communist legacy took office on Thursday after parliament backed its pledges to speed up market-oriented change.
"This is another kind of government, capable and willing to change Romania's fate," Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said after taking the oath in the Cotroceni presidential palace.
"A government that will fight poverty and catch the train of history moving towards integration into NATO and Europe."

The government is the offspring of a pact struck after Emil Constantinescu and his centrist allies forced ex-Communists from government for the first time since 1989 in presidential and general elections last month.

Most jobs went to the president's Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc and its Social Democratic coalition partners. Also included for the first time in the post-communist era were two leaders of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians.
The government's programme, overwhelmingly approved by parliament on Wednesday, is short on specific economic targets.

It calls for elimination of mass poverty which has pushed living standards below those in ex-communist Poland and Hungary, cautious monetary policy, less restrictive capital and currency markets and more benefits for the needy.
A trade unionist with a reputation as a corruption buster while Bucharest mayor, Ciorbea formally took over from outgoing Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu at his first cabinet session.
He heads a 27-man team resolved to buck the odds by securing NATO membership in the first wave of expansion next year and pressing on to join the European Union.

Leftist politicians, now on the opposition benches, say the programme lacks substance. But a top International Monetary Fund negotiator in Bucharest for the past week praised ministers' public commitment to reform.

Spearheading economic change will be two leaders of the National Peasant Party, the mainstay of the president's Convention. Mircea Ciumara, Finance Minister has set restoring morale among government functionaries as his top priority.
Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu admires Polish-style rapid privatisation and is considering plans to merge several institutions now responsible for sell-offs.

Foreign Minister Adrian Severin oversaw reforms under Petre Roman, Romania's first post-communist Prime Minister. He later raised eyebrows by opposing Russia's entry into the Council of Europe because of its campaign against separatist Chechnya.

Taking over at the defence ministry is law professor Victor Babiuc, who served as interior and then justice minister in 1991-92. Both he and Severin were political science professors during the 18-year reign of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Another returnee is Transport Minister Traian Basescu, who gets back the job he held in the early 1990s.
The new Information Minister, Radu Boroianu, is a theatre director and Culture Minister Ion Caramitru, an actor.
Caramitru gained fame for riding through Bucharest streets aboard an armoured car during the 1989 revolution and being one of the first to announce Ceausescu's overthrow on television.
